1. Publication Volume & Temporal Distribution

This section examines the monthly and yearly distribution of 4,886 biomedical research publications indexed in PubMed from January 2024 through March 2026. Understanding temporal patterns is essential for interpreting research output trends and avoiding misreadings caused by indexing lag.

Indexing Lag Advisory: Approximately 80% of records originate from 2024. This dominance reflects real-world PubMed indexing patterns where older publications accumulate more indexed entries over time, not an actual decline in research output. Data for 2025 and especially 2026 should be interpreted as partial snapshots.
Figure 1.1 — Monthly publication volume, Jan 2024 – Mar 2026. The declining curve reflects PubMed indexing lag, not a contraction in research output.
Figure 1.2 — Total publications by year. The 2024 dominance is an expected artifact of cumulative indexing.

Key Observations

  • 2024 accounts for 80.3% of all records (3,924 publications), consistent with the documented ~80% skew from cumulative PubMed indexing.
  • 2025 represents 15.1% of records (737 publications), and 2026 (Jan–Mar) represents 4.6% (225 publications).
  • The monthly trend shows a natural tapering pattern from early 2024 onward, with a steeper drop-off after mid-2025 as indexing lag compounds.
  • No strong seasonal periodicity is observed within complete-year data (2024), suggesting biomedical research output is relatively uniform across months after accounting for indexing pipelines.

3. Research Topic & MeSH Keyword Analysis

MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) indexing provides a structured lens into the thematic focus of biomedical research. This section identifies the most prevalent major topics, highlights the fastest-growing research areas, and maps keyword frequency patterns.

Note on Missing MeSH Data: Newer publications (particularly from 2025–2026) may not yet be MeSH-indexed, meaning topic and keyword analyses are weighted toward earlier records. This should be considered when interpreting growth metrics.
Figure 3.1 — Top 20 major MeSH topics by publication count. Dominant topics reflect core biomedical research priorities.

Emerging Topics — Acceleration Analysis

Identifying topics with the highest year-over-year growth rate surfaces emerging research frontiers. The following analysis compares 2024 and 2025 publication counts for each major topic, highlighting those with the steepest upward trajectory.

Figure 3.2 — Fastest-growing MeSH topics by 2024→2025 year-over-year growth rate. Red bars indicate >100% growth; green bars indicate <100% growth.

MeSH Keyword Frequency

Beyond major topics, individual MeSH descriptor terms provide a finer-grained view of the research themes permeating the literature. The most frequent keywords often reflect both disease-specific and methodological focus areas.

Figure 3.3 — Top 20 MeSH keywords by frequency across all publications with available keyword data.

Key Observations

  • COVID-19 is the most prevalent major topic with 43 publications, underscoring its centrality to current biomedical research.
  • The fastest-growing topic, N/A, shows a +0% year-over-year growth rate (2024→2025), signaling a rapidly expanding research frontier.
  • Keyword analysis reveals that foundational terms such as "Humans," "Animals," and methodological descriptors dominate frequency rankings, while disease-specific terms capture thematic specialization.
  • Emerging topic growth rates should be interpreted cautiously for topics with small base counts, where modest absolute gains produce large percentage increases.

4. Open Access Adoption & Journal Landscape

Open access (OA) publishing — defined here as availability via PubMed Central (PMC) — is a policy-sensitive metric with direct implications for research visibility, equity, and compliance with funder mandates. This section quantifies OA rates over time, across geographies, and by research type.

Figure 4.1 — Monthly open access rate trend. The dashed red line indicates the overall OA rate (65.1%).
Figure 4.2 — Left: OA rate by year. Right: OA rate by country for the top 10 contributing nations. Green = above overall OA rate; red = below.

Top Journals by Publication Volume

Figure 4.3 — Top 15 journals by publication volume in the dataset.

Key Observations

  • The overall open access rate stands at 65.1%, with year-over-year changes reflecting both genuine shifts in publishing norms and the composition effects of indexing lag.
  • OA rates vary substantially by country, suggesting that national funder mandates and institutional OA infrastructure play a significant role in adoption.
  • The journal landscape is diversified, with no single journal dominating output, indicating broad distribution across the biomedical publishing ecosystem.
  • Temporal trends in OA rate should be monitored as policy-sensitive indicators — increasing OA adoption may signal the impact of funder mandates and Plan S-aligned policies.

Key Observations

  • Journal Article is the dominant research type, accounting for the majority of publications. Reviews and Case Reports form the next most common categories.
  • The global median of 6 authors per publication serves as a baseline for collaboration intensity. Countries with higher medians may indicate more team-based or multi-institutional research cultures.
  • Author count distributions are right-skewed, with a long tail of highly collaborative publications involving 10+ authors, typical of large-scale clinical or multi-center studies.
  • Variation in collaboration intensity across countries may reflect differences in research infrastructure, funding models, and disciplinary focus.

6. Key Takeaways & Strategic Implications

The following synthesis distills the most actionable findings from this analysis, prioritized for research policy and funding strategy decision-making.

1. Indexing Lag Distorts Temporal Perception — Normalize Before Comparing

The 80% concentration of records in 2024 is an artifact of PubMed indexing pipelines, not a real output decline. Any year-over-year volume comparisons must account for this skew. Policy analysts should use normalized metrics (e.g., monthly averages within complete years) rather than raw totals when assessing growth or contraction.

2. N/A Is the Fastest-Accelerating Research Frontier

With a +0% year-over-year growth rate (2024→2025), N/A represents the most dynamic area of biomedical research output. Funding agencies and institutional strategists should consider whether this acceleration signals an unmet need or an emerging opportunity requiring targeted investment.

3. Geographic Concentration Is Moderate — Emerging Nations Are Gaining Share

The top 10 countries produce 48.1% of output, but the remaining share is distributed across a wide range of nations. Shifts in proportional representation across years suggest that emerging research ecosystems are gradually increasing their presence, which may warrant differentiated support strategies.

4. Open Access Adoption at 65.1% — Policy Momentum Is Building

The current OA rate reflects both the impact of funder mandates and the baseline of voluntary OA adoption. Continued monitoring of this metric is essential for evaluating the effectiveness of Plan S and similar policies. The variation in OA rates across countries suggests that national policy environments significantly influence adoption.

5. Collaboration Intensity Varies by Geography — Infrastructure Matters

Median author counts range from 5 to 8 across the top 10 countries, indicating meaningful differences in collaborative research culture. Higher collaboration intensity often correlates with multi-center studies and larger grant-funded projects — areas where strategic investment can amplify output.

Methodology & Data Notes

  • Data Source: 4,886 biomedical research abstracts from NCBI PubMed (Jan 2024 – Mar 2026), sourced from the Kaggle dataset "biomedical-research-abstracts-2024-2026" (kanchana1990).
  • Temporal Skew: The ~80% concentration of records in 2024 reflects cumulative PubMed indexing patterns. 2025–2026 data should be treated as partial.
  • Unknown Months: Records with pub_month_num = 0 were excluded from monthly trend analyses but included in yearly aggregations.
  • Missing MeSH: Records without major_topic or keywords were excluded from topic and keyword analyses. Newer publications are less likely to be MeSH-indexed.
  • Research Types: Multi-value research_type fields were split on delimiters; a single publication may contribute to multiple type categories.
  • Geography: Country represents first-author affiliation only, which may underrepresent international collaboration.
  • Growth Rates: YoY growth rates for emerging topics are calculated on raw counts and should be interpreted cautiously for topics with small base volumes.
